claim: ICOSL is constitutively expressed on APCs, such as dendritic cells (DCs), macrophages, and B cells.
source: ICOSL is constitutively expressed on APCs, such as dendritic cells (DCs), macrophages, and B cells, and it is strongly upregulated by inflammatory stimuli (Aicher et al., 2000; Swallow et al., 1999; Yoshinaga et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Aicher et al., 2000; Swallow et al., 1999; Yoshinaga et al., 2000).

claim: ICOSL is strongly upregulated by inflammatory stimuli.
source: ICOSL is constitutively expressed on APCs, such as dendritic cells (DCs), macrophages, and B cells, and it is strongly upregulated by inflammatory stimuli (Aicher et al., 2000; Swallow et al., 1999; Yoshinaga et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Aicher et al., 2000; Swallow et al., 1999; Yoshinaga et al., 2000).

claim: ICOSL is induced on non-lymphoid cells, such as endothelial cells or epithelial cells.
source: ICOSL presents a different expression profile as compared to CD80 and CD86, and it is induced on non-lymphoid cells, such as endothelial cells or epithelial cells (Khayyamian et al., 2002; Qian et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Khayyamian et al., 2002; Qian et al., 2006).

claim: The ICOS:ICOSL receptor pathway leads to enhanced T-cell activation, proliferation, and Th2 responses.
source: The ICOS:ICOSL receptor pathway leads to enhanced T-cell activation, proliferation, and Th2 responses (Riley et al., 2002; Tesciuba et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Riley et al., 2002; Tesciuba et al., 2001).

claim: ICOS is more relevant for the regulation of activated and effector T cells, in contrast to CD28, which is essential for the activation of naïve T cells.
source: In contrast to CD28, which is essential for the activation of naïve T cells, ICOS is more relevant for the regulation of activated and effector T cells (Coyle et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Coyle et al., 2000).

claim: ICOS co-stimulation plays an essential role in T-dependent antibody responses and germinal center (GC) formation.
source: In addition, ICOS co-stimulation plays an essential role in T-dependent antibody responses and germinal center (GC) formation, by inducing IL-21 production and Bcl6 expression, consequently controlling isotype switching, somatic hypermutation, and the generation of memory B cells and plasma cells (Choi et al., 2011; Hutloff, 2015; Liu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Choi et al., 2011; Hutloff, 2015; Liu et al., 2015).

claim: ICOS has been shown to be required for optimal CD8+ T-cell proliferation and cytokine production during recall responses.
source: ICOS has also been shown to be required for optimal CD8+ T-cell proliferation and cytokine production during recall responses (Takahashi et al., 2009; Wallin et al., 2001) and NK cell activation (Ogasawara et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Takahashi et al., 2009; Wallin et al., 2001).

claim: ICOS is required for NK cell activation.
source: ICOS has also been shown to be required for optimal CD8+ T-cell proliferation and cytokine production during recall responses (Takahashi et al., 2009; Wallin et al., 2001) and NK cell activation (Ogasawara et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Ogasawara et al., 2002).

claim: Different members of the herpesvirus family have been reported to disrupt the interaction established by co-signaling molecules in infected APCs and their counter receptors, in particular by downregulating CD80 and CD86.
source: Among them, different members of the herpesvirus family have been reported to disrupt the interaction established by co-signaling molecules in infected APCs and their counter receptors, in particular by downregulating CD80 and CD86.
evidence: Stated as a general observation about herpesviruses.

claim: Human and murine cytomegaloviruses (HCMV and MCMV, respectively) cause the downregulation of CD80 and CD86 during their respective infectious courses.
source: This is the case for example of the human and murine cytomegaloviruses (HCMV and MCMV, respectively), which cause the downregulation of these two molecules during their respective infectious courses (Hertel et al., 2003; Loewendorf et al., 2004; Mintern et al., 2006; Moutaftsi et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Hertel et al., 2003; Loewendorf et al., 2004; Mintern et al., 2006; Moutaftsi et al., 2002).

claim: MCMV infection causes a pronounced downmodulation of ICOSL in GFP+ infected peritoneal macrophages as compared with uninfected GFP- cells from the same cultures, or with mock-infected samples.
source: Notably, a pronounced downmodulation of ICOSL was also observed in GFP+ infected cells as compared with uninfected GFP- cells from the same cultures, or with mock-infected samples (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: ICOSL levels decreased to almost undetectable levels in MCMV-infected peritoneal macrophages.
source: Indeed, ICOSL levels decreased to almost undetectable levels, whereas the expression of the adhesion molecule CD62L, used as a negative control, remained unaffected.
evidence: Supported by experimental data described in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The expression of the adhesion molecule CD62L remained unaffected in MCMV-infected peritoneal macrophages.
source: Indeed, ICOSL levels decreased to almost undetectable levels, whereas the expression of the adhesion molecule CD62L, used as a negative control, remained unaffected.
evidence: Supported by experimental data described in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The surface reduction of ICOSL in MCMV-infected BMMs and BMDCs was significant.
source: Importantly, while robust expression of ICOSL was observed on all uninfected (mock or GFP-) cells, the surface reduction of this molecule in MCMV-infected BMMs and BMDCs was significant (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: MCMV infection causes downregulation of ICOSL on the macrophage cell line IC-21, the DC line DC2.4, and the endothelial cell line SVEC4-10.
source: Similar results were also obtained upon infection of the macrophage cell line IC-21, the DC line DC2.4, and the endothelial cell line SVEC4-10, although the extent of downregulation differed between them (Figure 1B), being quite dramatic on the IC-21 and DC2.4 cells, and more subtle in the SVEC4-10.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: De novo viral protein synthesis is required for ICOSL downregulation by MCMV.
source: To this end, peritoneal macrophages were infected for 72 hr (infection rates, approximately 90%) with UV-inactivated MCMV, and the results showed no loss of ICOSL surface expression (Figure 1C), indicating that a productive MCMV infection was required to alter ICOSL expression.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: By 4 hr post-infection (hpi) the density of ICOSL at the cell surface of peritoneal macrophages was substantially reduced.
source: As shown in Figure 1D, by 4 hr post-infection (hpi) the density of ICOSL at the cell surface was substantially reduced, and by 6 hpi there was barely any ICOSL at the surface of infected cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: By 6 hpi there was barely any ICOSL at the surface of MCMV-infected peritoneal macrophages.
source: As shown in Figure 1D, by 4 hr post-infection (hpi) the density of ICOSL at the cell surface was substantially reduced, and by 6 hpi there was barely any ICOSL at the surface of infected cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: In BMDC, the downregulation of ICOSL by MCMV begins to be evident by 8 hpi.
source: When a similar kinetics was conducted in BMDC and IC-21 cells, the downregulation of ICOSL differed with respect to timing, beginning to be evident by 8 hpi and 16 hpi, respectively, with the effect becoming more prominent from that time point onwards.
evidence: Supported by experimental data described in the text and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: In IC-21 cells, the downregulation of ICOSL by MCMV begins to be evident by 16 hpi.
source: When a similar kinetics was conducted in BMDC and IC-21 cells, the downregulation of ICOSL differed with respect to timing, beginning to be evident by 8 hpi and 16 hpi, respectively, with the effect becoming more prominent from that time point onwards.
evidence: Supported by experimental data described in the text and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: MCMV encodes one or more proteins to rapidly lower cell surface levels of ICOSL upon infection of APCs.
source: Thus, we concluded that MCMV encodes one or more proteins to rapidly lower cell surface levels of ICOSL upon infection of APCs.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing that UV-inactivated virus does not downregulate ICOSL and that downregulation occurs rapidly after infection.

claim: All MCMV mutants tested except for the deletion mutant MCMVΔm128-138 resulted in the marked downmodulation of ICOSL expression.
source: We found that, except for the deletion mutant MCMVΔm128-138, all MCMV mutants tested resulted in the marked downmodulation of ICOSL expression (Figure 2A; see as an example results for the MCMVΔm1-17 mutant).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The m138 protein is originally described as an Fc receptor.
source: The viral region deleted in MCMVΔm128-138, expanding from ORF m128 to m138, includes some ORFs with functions still unassigned and others involved in viral-host interactions, such as the m129/m131 chemokine homolog associated with tropism to macrophages (Fleming et al., 1999; Stahl et al., 2015), or the m138 protein, originally described as an Fc receptor (Thäle et al., 1994), and later reported to be also implicated in the reduction of cell surface expression of the NKG2D ligands H60, MULT-1, and RAE-1ε (Arapović et al., 2009; Lenac et al., 2006), and interestingly, of the co-stimulatory molecule CD80 (Mintern et al., 2006), a member of the B7 family to which also ICOSL belongs.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Thäle et al., 1994).

claim: The m138 protein is implicated in the reduction of cell surface expression of the NKG2D ligands H60, MULT-1, and RAE-1ε.
source: The viral region deleted in MCMVΔm128-138, expanding from ORF m128 to m138, includes some ORFs with functions still unassigned and others involved in viral-host interactions, such as the m129/m131 chemokine homolog associated with tropism to macrophages (Fleming et al., 1999; Stahl et al., 2015), or the m138 protein, originally described as an Fc receptor (Thäle et al., 1994), and later reported to be also implicated in the reduction of cell surface expression of the NKG2D ligands H60, MULT-1, and RAE-1ε (Arapović et al., 2009; Lenac et al., 2006), and interestingly, of the co-stimulatory molecule CD80 (Mintern et al., 2006), a member of the B7 family to which also ICOSL belongs.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Arapović et al., 2009; Lenac et al., 2006).

claim: The m138 protein is implicated in the reduction of cell surface expression of the co-stimulatory molecule CD80.
source: The viral region deleted in MCMVΔm128-138, expanding from ORF m128 to m138, includes some ORFs with functions still unassigned and others involved in viral-host interactions, such as the m129/m131 chemokine homolog associated with tropism to macrophages (Fleming et al., 1999; Stahl et al., 2015), or the m138 protein, originally described as an Fc receptor (Thäle et al., 1994), and later reported to be also implicated in the reduction of cell surface expression of the NKG2D ligands H60, MULT-1, and RAE-1ε (Arapović et al., 2009; Lenac et al., 2006), and interestingly, of the co-stimulatory molecule CD80 (Mintern et al., 2006), a member of the B7 family to which also ICOSL belongs.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Mintern et al., 2006).

claim: During infection of IC-21 cells with MCMVΔm138, cell surface expression of ICOSL was maintained to levels similar to mock-infected cells.
source: As illustrated in Figure 2B, during infection of IC-21 cells with MCMVΔm138, cell surface expression of ICOSL was maintained to levels similar to mock-infected cells, while the levels of CD84, a molecule targeted by the MCMV m154 protein (Strazic Geljic et al., 2020), used as a control, markedly decreased.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: One gene product, m138, is responsible for the complete downregulation of ICOSL during MCMV infection.
source: These results revealed that one gene product, m138, is responsible for the complete downregulation of ICOSL during MCMV infection.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing that MCMVΔm138 does not downregulate ICOSL.

claim: m138 is able to exert its downmodulatory effects on ICOSL expression without requiring the MCMV infection context.
source: Therefore, these results indicate that m138 is able to exert its downmodulatory effects on ICOSL expression without requiring the MCMV infection context.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from transfection assays shown in Figure 2C.

claim: m138 has been predicted to be a 569-aa type I transmembrane glycoprotein.
source: m138 has been predicted to be a 569-aa type I transmembrane glycoprotein (Thäle et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Thäle et al., 1994).

claim: The m138 viral protein was detected in perinuclear compartments and cytoplasmic 'large punctate vesicles' in GFP+ infected cells.
source: As shown in Figure 3A (panels a-c and g), using permeabilizing conditions, the viral protein was detected in perinuclear compartments and cytoplasmic 'large punctate vesicles' in GFP+ infected cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In non-permeabilized infected cells, the mAb against m138 failed to detect the viral protein at the cell surface.
source: In contrast, in non-permeabilized infected cells, the mAb against m138 failed to detect the viral protein at the cell surface (Figure 3A, panels d-f), whereas it could be recognized at this location in the 300.19 cells stably transfected with HA-m138 (Figure 3C, left panels).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A dim expression of m138 at the cell surface of infected cells could be observed by flow cytometry.
source: When analyzed by flow cytometry, though, a dim expression of m138 at the cell surface of infected cells could be observed (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: m138 colocalized with lysosomes in MCMV-infected NIH3T3 cells.
source: The results, illustrated in Figure 3D (panels c, and d), indicated that m138 colocalized with lysosomes.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Quantification of the m138/lysosome colocalization led to Manders colocalization coefficients of M1 = 0.76 and M2 = 0.80.
source: Indeed, quantification of the m138/lysosome colocalization, using the Coloc2 plugin from FIJI/ImageJ program, led to Manders colocalization coefficients of M1 = 0.76 and M2 = 0.80.
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of experimental data.

claim: In MCMV-infected cell lysates, the 70 kDa band of ICOSL was drastically reduced.
source: Notably, in MCMV-infected cell lysates, the 70 kDa band was drastically reduced (lane 4), whereas it was not substantially altered after infection with MCMVΔm138 (lane 5), suggesting that this band corresponds to the mature surface form of ICOSL.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The 70 kDa band of ICOSL corresponds to the mature surface form of ICOSL.
source: Notably, in MCMV-infected cell lysates, the 70 kDa band was drastically reduced (lane 4), whereas it was not substantially altered after infection with MCMVΔm138 (lane 5), suggesting that this band corresponds to the mature surface form of ICOSL.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing that the 70 kDa band is reduced by MCMV infection and is sensitive to trypsin treatment.

claim: m138 was altering the expression of the mature form of ICOSL that reaches the cell surface.
source: Thus, m138 was altering the expression of the mature form of ICOSL that reaches the cell surface.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing that the 70 kDa band is reduced by MCMV infection and is sensitive to trypsin treatment.

claim: MCMV infection initially induces ICOSL expression and m138 subsequently leads to the depletion of cell-surface ICOSL, but not of the overall intracellular levels of this molecule.
source: Thus, MCMV infection initially induces ICOSL expression and m138 subsequently leads to the depletion of cell-surface ICOSL, but not of the overall intracellular levels of this molecule.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing that the 51 kDa band is more abundant in infected samples and that UV-inactivated MCMV induces ICOSL expression.

claim: HCMV infection of primary monocyte-derived macrophages or differentiated THP-1 cells results in a strong ICOSL cell surface downregulation.
source: However, we demonstrate that following a productive HCMV infection of primary monocyte-derived macrophages or differentiated THP-1 cells, which express high levels of ICOSL, a strong ICOSL cell surface downregulation also takes place, and that this process requires viral gene expression.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 11A.

claim: HCMV downregulation of ICOSL requires viral gene expression.
source: However, we demonstrate that following a productive HCMV infection of primary monocyte-derived macrophages or differentiated THP-1 cells, which express high levels of ICOSL, a strong ICOSL cell surface downregulation also takes place, and that this process requires viral gene expression.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 11C.

claim: HCMV leads to diminished cell surface ICOSL and to an abrogation of its expression in whole cell levels, via a lysosomal degradation-independent process.
source: Our findings also indicate that HCMV not only leads to diminished cell surface ICOSL, but also to an abrogation of its expression in whole cell levels, via a lysosomal degradation-independent process.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 11D.

claim: A similar complete loss of ICOSL on differentiated THP-1 cells was observed during infection by two α-herpesviruses, HSV-1 and HSV-2.
source: Importantly, a similar complete loss of ICOSL on differentiated THP-1 cells was observed during infection by two α-herpesviruses, HSV-1 and HSV-2.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 11E and 11F.

claim: In cells co-transfected with the m138-GFP protein, the 70 kDa ICOSL band, corresponding to ICOSL on the cell surface, was not observed.
source: As shown in Figure 5A, in cells co-transfected with the m138-GFP protein, independently of whether or not the lysosomal inhibitor treatment was applied, the 70 kDa ICOSL band, corresponding to ICOSL on the cell surface, was not observed (lanes 4 and 5).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The 51 kDa band of ICOSL augmented (1.5-fold) after exposure to leupeptin and bafilomycin in cells co-transfected with m138-GFP.
source: In addition, the results also evidenced that the 51 kDa band, corresponding to intracellular ICOSL, augmented (1.5-fold) after exposure to leupeptin and bafilomycin (compare lanes 4 and 5).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The viral protein m138 was targeting ICOSL before reaching the cell surface.
source: The presence of the 70 kDa mature form of ICOSL when the CTL-GFP was expressed, and its absence upon expression of m138-GFP under conditions of lysosomal inhibition, pointed out that the viral protein was targeting ICOSL before reaching the cell surface.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing that the 70 kDa band is absent when m138 is expressed even with lysosomal inhibition.

claim: A marked colocalization of ICOSL and the m138 viral protein in perinuclear compartments and in cytoplasmic punctate structures could be observed in MCMV-infected NIH3T3 HA-ICOSL cells.
source: We then infected NIH3T3 HA-ICOSL cells with MCMVwt and examined by confocal fluorescence microscopy m138 and ICOSL expression. A marked colocalization of ICOSL and the viral protein in perinuclear compartments and in cytoplasmic punctate structures could be observed, being more robust after treatment with the lysosomal inhibitors (Figure 5B, panels g and h).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The expression signal of ICOSL was increased after treatment with leupeptin and bafilomycin in MCMV-infected NIH3T3 HA-ICOSL cells.
source: Accordingly, the expression signal of ICOSL was also increased after treatment with leupeptin and bafilomycin (compare panels a and e in Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The levels of m138 augmented upon exposure to the lysosomal inhibitors in MCMV-infected NIH3T3 HA-ICOSL cells.
source: The results also showed augmented levels of m138 upon exposure to the lysosomal inhibitors (compare panels b and f), indicating that m138 was getting partially co-degraded with its target.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: m138 was getting partially co-degraded with its target ICOSL.
source: The results also showed augmented levels of m138 upon exposure to the lysosomal inhibitors (compare panels b and f), indicating that m138 was getting partially co-degraded with its target.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing that m138 levels increase with lysosomal inhibition.

claim: m138 precludes the maturation of ICOSL by targeting it to lysosomes.
source: Collectively, the data suggest that m138 precludes the maturation of ICOSL by targeting it to lysosomes, explaining how the levels of this co-signaling molecule are decreased at the cell surface.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing colocalization with lysosomes and increased ICOSL levels with lysosomal inhibition.

claim: The m138 protein was recovered when the immunoprecipitation was carried out with the anti-HA antibody in NIH3T3 cells transiently expressing m138-GFP and HA-ICOSL.
source: As illustrated in Figure 5D, the m138 protein was recovered when the immunoprecipitation was carried out with the anti-HA antibody (lane 2), whereas when using the antibody against human Fc the viral protein was not detected (lane 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: m138, either directly or in an indirect manner, associates with ICOSL.
source: These data suggest that m138, either directly or in an indirect manner, associates with ICOSL.
evidence: Inferred from co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The ectodomain of m138 is predicted to be composed by three Ig-like domains.
source: The ectodomain of m138 is predicted to be composed by three Ig-like domains (Lenac et al., 2006; Corrales-Aguilar et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Lenac et al., 2006; Corrales-Aguilar et al., 2014).

claim: The m138ΔIg1-GFP protein was incapable to significantly reduce ICOSL or CD80 cell surface levels.
source: As shown in Figure 6B, the m138ΔIg1-GFP protein was incapable to significantly reduce ICOSL or CD80 cell surface levels.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: CD80 surface density decreased in cells transfected with m138ΔIg2-GFP and m138ΔIg2/3-GFP.
source: In contrast, while CD80 surface density decreased in cells transfected with m138ΔIg2-GFP and m138ΔIg2/3-GFP, these two m138 mutants did not alter in a substantial manner ICOSL expression.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The m138ΔIg2-GFP and m138ΔIg2/3-GFP mutants did not alter in a substantial manner ICOSL expression.
source: In contrast, while CD80 surface density decreased in cells transfected with m138ΔIg2-GFP and m138ΔIg2/3-GFP, these two m138 mutants did not alter in a substantial manner ICOSL expression.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The Ig1 domain of m138 is absolutely required for both ICOSL and CD80 downregulation.
source: Therefore, we conclude that the Ig1 domain of m138 is absolutely required for both ICOSL and CD80 downregulation.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing that m138ΔIg1 does not downregulate ICOSL or CD80.

claim: The putative Ig2 and Ig3 domains of m138 need to be preserved for the downregulation of ICOSL, but they are dispensable for m138-mediated decrease of CD80 expression.
source: However, while the putative Ig2 and Ig3 domains of m138 need to be preserved for the downregulation of ICOSL, they are dispensable for m138-mediated decrease of CD80 expression.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing that m138ΔIg2 and m138ΔIg2/3 downregulate CD80 but not ICOSL.

claim: Infections with MCMVm138ΔIg2 or MCMVm138ΔIg2/Ig3 led to decreased cell-surface density of CD80 but not ICOSL.
source: As it occurred in transfection assays with the m138 mutant plasmids defective in these Ig domains, infections with MCMVm138ΔIg2 or MCMVm138ΔIg2/Ig3 led to decreased cell-surface density of CD80 but not ICOSL (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Both MCMVm138ΔIg2 and MCMVm138ΔIg2/Ig3-infected BMDCs stimulated significantly stronger IFN-γ responses by CD8+ T cells as compared to the MCMVwt-infected cells.
source: Remarkably, as illustrated in Figure 7B, both MCMVm138ΔIg2 and MCMVm138ΔIg2/Ig3-infected BMDCs stimulated significantly stronger IFN-γ responses by CD8+ T cells as compared to the MCMVwt-infected cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The magnitude of the IFN-γ induction observed with MCMVm138ΔIg2 and MCMVm138ΔIg2/Ig3 almost approached the levels obtained in MCMVΔm138-infected BDMCs.
source: Moreover, the magnitude of the IFN-γ induction observed with these two MCMV mutants, which downregulated CD80 but preserved cell surface levels of ICOSL intact, almost approached the levels obtained in MCMVΔm138-infected BDMCs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The m138 protein contributes substantially to the evasion of the CD8+ T-cell immune response via manipulation of the ICOSL:ICOS axis.
source: These findings provide evidence for a substantial contribution of the m138 protein in the evasion of the CD8+ T-cell immune response via manipulation of the ICOSL:ICOS axis (Figure 7B).
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing that MCMV mutants that preserve ICOSL induce stronger CD8+ T cell responses.

claim: A significant reduction of ICOSL levels was observed on the surface of the GFP+ MCMV-infected peritoneal macrophages as compared to the uninfected GFP- macrophages in vivo.
source: As shown in Figure 8A, we observed a significant reduction of ICOSL levels, in parallel to those of MHC I used as a positive control, on the surface of the GFP+ MCMV-infected as compared to the uninfected GFP- macrophages.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: A marked MCMVwt-induced downmodulation of ICOSL on peritoneal DCs was observed in vivo.
source: Figure 8B illustrates a marked MCMVwt-induced downmodulation of ICOSL on peritoneal DCs, and a subsequent significant augmentation of the levels of this molecule in the absence of m138, on the surface of MCMVΔm138-infected peritoneal DCs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: A significant augmentation of the levels of ICOSL was observed in the absence of m138, on the surface of MCMVΔm138-infected peritoneal DCs in vivo.
source: Figure 8B illustrates a marked MCMVwt-induced downmodulation of ICOSL on peritoneal DCs, and a subsequent significant augmentation of the levels of this molecule in the absence of m138, on the surface of MCMVΔm138-infected peritoneal DCs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: A clear increase of CD80 levels was detected on MCMVΔm138-infected peritoneal DCs when compared to both mock-infected and MCMVwt-infected DCs in vivo.
source: In the case of CD80, although the downmodulation caused by MCMVwt was subtle, a clear increase of CD80 levels was detected on MCMVΔm138-infected cells when compared to both mock-infected and MCMVwt-infected DCs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: m138 plays a role in downmodulating ICOSL and CD80 on primary mouse DCs in vivo.
source: Therefore, these results confirmed a role of m138 downmodulating ICOSL and CD80 on primary mouse DCs (Figure 8B).
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing that MCMVΔm138 does not downregulate ICOSL and CD80 on DCs in vivo.

claim: In the salivary glands, viral titers of MCMVm138ΔIg2 were lower than those of MCMVwt.
source: As illustrated in Figure 8D, in the salivary glands, viral titers of MCMVm138ΔIg2, a mutant which is unable to downregulate H60 and ICOSL, were lower than those of MCMVwt.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The MCMVm138ΔIg2 titers in salivary glands were below the detection limits for all animals, in a similar way as in MCMVΔm138 infected mice.
source: In fact, the MCMVm138ΔIg2 titers in this organ were below the detection limits for all animals, in a similar way as in MCMVΔm138 infected mice.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: MCMVm138ΔIg2 was still heavily attenuated as compared to MCMVwt under conditions of NK cell depletion in salivary glands.
source: NK cell depletion led to a substantial increase of both MCMVΔm138 and MCMVm138ΔIg2 infection in this organ, but importantly, MCMVm138ΔIg2, which was downmodulating CD80 but not ICOSL, was still heavily attenuated as compared to MCMVwt under these conditions.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: ICOSL targeting by m138 is important for the virus to increase its load in salivary glands.
source: This finding indicated that ICOSL targeting by m138 is important for the virus to increase its load in salivary glands.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing that MCMVm138ΔIg2, which does not downregulate ICOSL, is attenuated in salivary glands.

claim: The downregulation of CD80 by m138 did not seem to play a major role during MCMV replication in salivary glands.
source: Conversely, the downregulation of CD80 by m138 did not seem to play a major role during MCMV replication in this organ.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing that MCMVm138ΔIg2, which downregulates CD80, is still attenuated.

claim: When NK cells together with CD4+ and CD8+ T cells were depleted, MCMVm138ΔIg2 growth in the salivary glands was completely restored.
source: Furthermore, when besides NK cells, CD4+ and CD8+ T cells were depleted, MCMVm138ΔIg2 growth in the salivary glands was completely restored, indicating that m138 via interference with ICOSL evades T-cell responses.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: m138 via interference with ICOSL evades T-cell responses.
source: Furthermore, when besides NK cells, CD4+ and CD8+ T cells were depleted, MCMVm138ΔIg2 growth in the salivary glands was completely restored, indicating that m138 via interference with ICOSL evades T-cell responses.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing that depletion of T cells restores MCMVm138ΔIg2 growth.

claim: A role of the viral m138 protein participating in immune evasion of CD4+ T cells could be observed in spleen and lungs when comparing data from MCMVwt and MCMVΔm138 infections.
source: The data, illustrated in Figure 8—figure supplement 1, show that the frequencies of CD4+ T cells increased in the three organs analyzed upon MCMV infection. Moreover, a role of the viral m138 protein participating in immune evasion of CD4+ T cells could be observed in spleen and lungs when comparing data from MCMVwt and MCMVΔm138 infections, although this was not the case in the salivary glands.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: A marked decrease of the percentage of Tfh cells in both spleen and lymph nodes was observed when infected mice were deprived of ICOSL-mediated signals.
source: As illustrated in Figure 9A, a marked decrease of the percentage of Tfh cells in both spleen and lymph nodes was observed when infected mice were deprived of ICOSL-mediated signals.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: GC B cells in lymph nodes were dramatically reduced upon ICOSL blockade.
source: In addition, while the percentage of follicular B cells was not substantially altered, or was even slightly higher, upon ICOSL blockade, GC B cells in lymph nodes were dramatically reduced.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: GCs were smaller in size in the infected mice that received anti-ICOSL antibody as compared to mice that did not received it.
source: Consistent with these observations, an analysis by immunofluorescence of splenic sections revealed that GCs were smaller in size in the infected mice that received anti-ICOSL antibody as compared to mice that did not received it, whereas this was not the case of the follicles, whose sizes seemed not to be affected by the treatment (Figure 9B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: The blockade of ICOSL resulted in an increased percentage of naïve CD4+ T cells in the spleen and decreased percentages of memory CD4+ T cells in spleens and lymph nodes.
source: In addition, the blockade of ICOSL also resulted in an increased percentage of naïve CD4+ T cells in the spleen and decreased percentages of memory CD4+ T cells in spleens and lymph nodes (Figure 9A), an indication that long lasting immune protection to MCMV could be also impaired in the absence of ICOSL:ICOS signaling.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Mice that received the anti-ICOSL antibody had significantly reduced levels of total IgG specific for MCMV than those that did not receive it.
source: We observed that mice that received the anti-ICOSL antibody had significantly reduced levels of total IgG specific for MCMV than those that did not receive it (Figure 10A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10A.

claim: A substantial decreased production of MCMV-specific IgG1 and IgG2a and b was detected in infected animals in which ICOSL was blocked.
source: When we evaluated the serum levels of the predominant subclasses of natural antibodies, a substantial decreased production of MCMV-specific IgG1 and IgG2a and b was detected in infected animals in which ICOSL was blocked, while no differences were found in the production of MCMV-specific IgG3 or IgM responses between both groups (Figure 10A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10A.

claim: No differences were found in the production of MCMV-specific IgG3 or IgM responses between mice that received anti-ICOSL antibody and those that did not.
source: When we evaluated the serum levels of the predominant subclasses of natural antibodies, a substantial decreased production of MCMV-specific IgG1 and IgG2a and b was detected in infected animals in which ICOSL was blocked, while no differences were found in the production of MCMV-specific IgG3 or IgM responses between both groups (Figure 10A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10A.

claim: ICOSL-mediated co-stimulation was crucial for the development of MCMV-specific IgG1 and IgG2 responses.
source: These results indicated that ICOSL-mediated co-stimulation was crucial for the development of MCMV-specific IgG1 and IgG2 responses.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing reduced IgG1 and IgG2 levels with ICOSL blockade.

claim: Sera from mice that received the anti-ICOSL antibody exhibited a significant lower capacity to neutralize MCMV compared to those that did not received it.
source: As illustrated in Figure 10B, sera from mice that received the anti-ICOSL antibody exhibited a significant lower capacity to neutralize MCMV compared to those that did not received it.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10B.

claim: ICOSL:ICOS interactions play a prominent role in the induction of effective T and B cell responses during MCMV infection.
source: In conclusion, our findings indicate a prominent role of ICOSL:ICOS interactions in the induction of effective T and B cell responses during MCMV infection.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing reduced T and B cell responses with ICOSL blockade.

claim: ICOSL downregulation is a strategy used by different herpesviruses.
source: Altogether, these findings demonstrate that ICOSL downregulation is a strategy used by different herpesviruses.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing ICOSL downregulation by MCMV, HCMV, HSV-1, and HSV-2.

claim: ICOSL-mediated co-stimulation contributes to the development of effective anti-MCMV immune responses.
source: Here, we report that ICOSL-mediated co-stimulation contributes to the development of effective anti-MCMV immune responses.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing reduced immune responses with ICOSL blockade.

claim: ICOSL constitutes a major target of CMVs and other herpesviruses, which potently downregulate its expression on the surface of APCs.
source: In addition, we demonstrate that ICOSL constitutes a major target of CMVs and other herpesviruses, which potently downregulate its expression on the surface of APCs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing ICOSL downregulation by multiple herpesviruses.

claim: MCMV uses its immunoevasin m138/fcr-1 to manipulate ICOSL, impeding a correct T-cell activation during acute MCMV infection.
source: We show that MCMV uses its immunoevasin m138/fcr-1 to manipulate this co-signaling molecule, impeding a correct T-cell activation during acute MCMV infection.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing that m138 downregulates ICOSL and impairs T-cell responses.

claim: m138 is a 69 kDa type I transmembrane glycoprotein, largely localized in the ER and lysosomal compartments.
source: m138 is a 69 kDa type I transmembrane glycoprotein, largely localized in the ER and lysosomal compartments, and shown to be further processed into a 105 kDa highly glycosylated form (Mintern et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Mintern et al., 2006).

claim: m138 is shown to be further processed into a 105 kDa highly glycosylated form.
source: m138 is a 69 kDa type I transmembrane glycoprotein, largely localized in the ER and lysosomal compartments, and shown to be further processed into a 105 kDa highly glycosylated form (Mintern et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Mintern et al., 2006).

claim: m138 was reported to perturb the endocytosis of surface RAE-1ε and MULT-1, interfering with the clathrin dependent endocytosis of MULT-1, altering its recycling and leading to its subsequent degradation in lysosomes.
source: Consistent with its location at the plasma membrane, the viral protein was shown to perturb the endocytosis of surface RAE-1ε and MULT-1, interfering with the clathrin dependent endocytosis of this later cellular target, altering its recycling and leading to its subsequent degradation in lysosomes (Arapović et al., 2009; Lenac et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Arapović et al., 2009; Lenac et al., 2006).

claim: A different mode of action was reported for m138 in the downregulation of CD80, targeting the cellular molecule when newly synthesized early in the secretory pathway and mislocalizing it to lysosomal compartments.
source: A different mode of action was reported for m138 in the downregulation of CD80, targeting the cellular molecule when newly synthesized early in the secretory pathway and mislocalizing it to lysosomal compartments (Mintern et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Mintern et al., 2006).

claim: MCMV produces the multifaceted immunomodulatory protein m152, which is capable of downregulating MHC class I molecules and different RAE-1 isoforms, as well as modulating the cGAS-STING pathway.
source: For instance, MCMV produces the multifaceted immunomodulatory protein m152, which is capable of downregulating MHC class I molecules and different RAE-1 isoforms, as well as modulating the cGAS-STING pathway, thereby evading type I IFN-, NK-, and T cell-dependent immune responses to MCMV infection (Fink et al., 2013; Krmpotic et al., 1999; Lodoen et al., 2003; Stempel et al., 2019; Ziegler et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Fink et al., 2013; Krmpotic et al., 1999; Lodoen et al., 2003; Stempel et al., 2019; Ziegler et al., 1997).

claim: By interfering with AP-1-mediated protein sorting, the m154 glycoprotein targets a broad-spectrum of cell surface molecules implicated in the antiviral NK and T-cell responses.
source: Moreover, we have recently demonstrated that by interfering with AP-1-mediated protein sorting, the m154 glycoprotein targets a broad-spectrum of cell surface molecules implicated in the antiviral NK and T-cell responses (Strazic Geljic et al., 2020; Zarama et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Strazic Geljic et al., 2020; Zarama et al., 2014).

claim: The CD80/CD86:CD28 co-stimulatory pathway has been shown to be also involved in the induction of Tfh cells and class switching of MCMV-specific antibodies.
source: Notably, while the CD80/CD86:CD28 co-stimulatory pathway has been shown to be also involved in the induction of Tfh cells and class switching of MCMV-specific antibodies, we find that this pathway is not capable to compensate the defects observed in the absence of ICOS signaling, evidencing the non-redundant role of the two axis in this scenario (Welten et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Welten et al., 2016).

claim: The CD80/CD86:CD28 co-stimulatory pathway is not capable to compensate the defects observed in the absence of ICOS signaling during MCMV infection.
source: Notably, while the CD80/CD86:CD28 co-stimulatory pathway has been shown to be also involved in the induction of Tfh cells and class switching of MCMV-specific antibodies, we find that this pathway is not capable to compensate the defects observed in the absence of ICOS signaling, evidencing the non-redundant role of the two axis in this scenario (Welten et al., 2016).
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing that ICOSL blockade leads to defects in Tfh and antibody responses.

claim: ICOS- and ICOSL-deficient patients have been associated with combined T- and B-cell immunodeficiency, and importantly, with an increased susceptibility to viral infections.
source: Of interest, ICOS- and ICOSL-deficient patients have been associated with combined T- and B-cell immunodeficiency, and importantly, with an increased susceptibility to viral infections (Roussel et al., 2018; Schepp et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Roussel et al., 2018; Schepp et al., 2017).

claim: A high incidence of recurrent herpesvirus infections, mostly including herpes simplex and cytomegalovirus infections, was observed in ICOS- and ICOSL-deficient patients.
source: Moreover, while the infectious phenotype of these patients varied, a high incidence of recurrent herpesvirus infections, mostly including herpes simplex and cytomegalovirus infections, was observed.
evidence: Stated as an observation about ICOS- and ICOSL-deficient patients.

claim: Deletion of m138 or both m138 and the CD86 downmodulator m147.5 from MCMV has a dramatic impact on viral load during acute infection.
source: It was previously shown that deletion of m138 or both m138 and the CD86 downmodulator m147.5 from MCMV has a dramatic impact on viral load during acute infection (Arens et al., 2011; Crnković-Mertens et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Arens et al., 2011; Crnković-Mertens et al., 1998).

claim: Downmodulation of ICOSL by m138 represents an effective immune evasion strategy during the acute MCMV infection.
source: Altogether, our results support the notion that downmodulation of ICOSL by m138 represents an effective immune evasion strategy during the acute MCMV infection.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing that MCMV mutants that do not downregulate ICOSL are attenuated.
